{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-sc-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"4d9db99e8a5418c9c2cf5aedee8ad273f6a356e548f9a0647f708baca10f308b","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-sc-class-d:lineage:64","source_registry_sha256":"61c32f86a25e3c021742b3c9ddf64a97709817dd75a19df6d2b69eac0a40c4f1","source_liveness_sha256":"feb7871590284d2a19ab0509ff65b48154ba15e637a6ec9b839f55a72736ffdb"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Special driving situations: night driving, work zones, rural roads, winter driving and towing a trailer","heading":"C — Headlight use and seeing at night, work zone conduct, rural road hazards, winter driving and getting unstuck, and loading, swaying and backing with a trailer","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Headlight use and seeing at night, work zone conduct, rural road hazards, winter driving and getting unstuck, and loading, swaying and backing with a trailer
Knowledge domain: how a South Carolina driver adjusts to darkness, work zones, rural roads, occasional snow and ice and towing a trailer, including the headlight distances, the extra following time at night, work zone duties, rural hazards, winter traction tips and the core trailer loading and handling rules; further trailer hookup and checklist facts continue in part C2.

FACT_ID: sec15-F01 | anchor: A01
Night driving is harder and more dangerous than daytime driving, because your headlights limit how far ahead you can see. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec15-F02 | anchor: A01
Use your high beams whenever there are no oncoming vehicles, since they let you see twice as far as low beams. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec15-F03 | anchor: A01
Lower your high beams while an oncoming vehicle is still at least 500 feet away. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec15-F04 | anchor: A01
If an oncoming vehicle keeps its high beams on, glance toward the right side of the road so you are not distracted or briefly blinded. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0125]

FACT_ID: sec15-F05 | anchor: A02
Use low beams when you are following another vehicle that is less than 200 feet ahead of you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-F06 | anchor: A02
In fog, rain or snow use low beams, because high beams can cause glare that makes it harder to see; some vehicles also have fog lights for these conditions. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-F07 | anchor: A02
Do not look straight into oncoming headlights; keep your eyes searching the road in front of you. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-F08 | anchor: A02
At night, search well beyond your headlight beams for dark shapes on the road, and glance left and right now and then to find the pavement edge and any hazards from the sides. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-F09 | anchor: A02
Do not wear sunglasses or colored lenses at night or on overcast days, because tinted lenses reduce your vision. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-F10 | anchor: A02
At night add at least one extra second to your following distance, and at least two extra seconds on unfamiliar roads at night. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0126]

FACT_ID: sec15-F11 | anchor: A03
A work zone is an area where roadwork is under way, and it may involve a lane closure, a detour and moving equipment. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-F12 | anchor: A03
The manual says approximately 40,000 people a year are injured in motor vehicle collisions in work zones. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-F13 | anchor: A03
Approaching a work zone, watch for signs, cones, barrels, large vehicles and workers, and remember that work zone signs have orange backgrounds with black letters or symbols. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-F14 | anchor: A03
Always slow down in a work zone even when no workers are present, because narrower lanes and rough pavement can make conditions hazardous. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-F15 | anchor: A03
Endangering a highway worker can bring a fine and points on your driving record, under SC Code §56-5-1535. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0127]

FACT_ID: sec15-F16 | anchor: A04
In a work zone, slow down, leave a longer following gap, keep track of surrounding traffic and be ready to stop. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec15-F17 | anchor: A04
Use extreme caution in a work zone at night, whether or not workers are present. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec15-F18 | anchor: A04
Shift your lane position to give workers and construction vehicles room, and keep obeying work zone signs until you see End Road Work. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0128]

FACT_ID: sec15-F19 | anchor: A05
On rural roads stay alert, watch for warning signs and obey the speed limit. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec15-F20 | anchor: A05
Gravel and dirt roads reduce traction, so slow down, leave more following distance and expect that you may skid when you stop. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec15-F21 | anchor: A05
Rural roads are often narrower, with ditches or drop-offs instead of shoulders, so slow down, keep centered in your lane and watch for oncoming traffic that may drift into it. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec15-F22 | anchor: A05
At narrow or single-lane bridges drivers take turns, and generally the first driver to reach the bridge has the right-of-way. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec15-F23 | anchor: A05
Open bridge gratings and steel bridges can reduce traction, so slow down, increase your following distance and hold the wheel firmly. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec15-F24 | anchor: A05
Blind corners created by woods, growing crops or steep hills limit how far you can see, so always slow down there and be ready to stop. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0129]

FACT_ID: sec15-F25 | anchor: A06
Some rural intersections have no stop or yield signs, so approach them slowly and be ready to stop for crossing or oncoming traffic. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec15-F26 | anchor: A06
South Carolina rarely has extreme winters but sometimes gets snow and ice, which call for slower speeds, acceleration, steering and braking. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec15-F27 | anchor: A06
Bridges, overpasses and lightly traveled roads tend to freeze first, and even above freezing, wet conditions can leave ice in shady spots or on exposed roads such as bridges. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec15-F28 | anchor: A06
If you must drive in snow or ice, tire chains or special snow tires are recommended, and you should keep the windshield and windows clear and use the defroster. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec15-F29 | anchor: A06
Extra weight loaded in the trunk can help a rear-wheel-drive car get traction. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0130]

FACT_ID: sec15-F30 | anchor: A07
Keep a full tank of gasoline in winter to prevent condensation inside the tank, which may freeze. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec15-F31 | anchor: A07
When you can, drive in the tracks left by earlier vehicles, and brake gently to slow down or stop on snow or ice. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec15-F32 | anchor: A07
Avoid using cruise control in winter driving conditions. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec15-F33 | anchor: A07
Leave extra room between you and other vehicles on snow or ice, remembering that ice patches may form on bridges even when the roads are clear. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec15-F34 | anchor: A07
Generally avoid hills in winter, and if you must use them, drive slowly at a steady pace with a good gap ahead, since restarting after stopping on a hill may be nearly impossible. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec15-F35 | anchor: A07
If your vehicle gets stuck in snow, do not spin the wheels; turn them from side to side a few times, use a light touch on the gas and shovel snow away from the wheels and underside. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0131]

FACT_ID: sec15-F36 | anchor: A08
If your vehicle skids on winter roads, lift your foot off the accelerator and steer toward where you want the front of the vehicle to go. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0132]

FACT_ID: sec15-F37 | anchor: A10
Load a trailer heavier in the front to reduce sway, since failing to do so is a leading cause of vehicle-trailer mishaps. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0134]

FACT_ID: sec15-F38 | anchor: A10
Put 60 percent of a trailer's cargo weight up front, closest to the towing vehicle, and the remaining 40 percent toward the rear. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0134]

FACT_ID: sec15-F39 | anchor: A10
If a trailer starts to sway or whip, steer straight and slow down gradually without braking, never speed up, and stop once you can get completely off the road. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0134]

FACT_ID: sec15-F40 | anchor: A11
The maximum recommended speed for most vehicle-trailer combinations is 55 mph, the posted limit must never be exceeded, and worse conditions call for even lower speeds. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0135]

FACT_ID: sec15-F41 | anchor: A12
When backing a trailer, go slowly with your hand at the bottom of the steering wheel, moving your hand left to send the trailer left and right to send it right. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0136]

FACT_ID: sec15-F42 | anchor: A12
If the trailer starts to jackknife, stop, pull ahead to straighten out and then start backing again. [A12]
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0136]

Misconceptions: high beams in fog, rain or snow make seeing harder, not easier; tinted lenses reduce vision at night; a work zone still calls for slowing when no workers are visible; ice can form above freezing on wet bridges and in shade; spinning your wheels digs a stuck car in deeper; braking during trailer sway makes things worse, so you steer straight and ease off.
Mnemonics: dim at five hundred feet for oncoming cars, low beams within two hundred feet behind another; add one second at night and two on strange roads at night; sixty in front, forty in back; to back a trailer, hand at the bottom moves the way the trailer should go.
Glossary: high beams means the bright headlight setting that lets you see twice as far as low beams; work zone means an area of roadwork with lane closures, detours or equipment; blind corner means a corner you cannot see around; uncontrolled intersection means one with no stop or yield signs; trailer sway means side-to-side whipping of a trailer; coupler and hitch ball mean the trailer and vehicle parts that lock together.
Dynamic facts: the yearly count of people injured in work zone collisions and the manual's national trailer towing mileage are statistics that change over time; refresh them before they are shown.
